Provenance note: Header prepended by the Library thread; the OCR text follows unchanged apart from this header. Nothing was corrected, re-spaced or retyped, and no characters were replaced. The fetched file is 1106645 bytes, the size the host lists for it; the end of the file was read. OCR sampled at opening, middle and end: The opening is the Rolls notice, readable apart from stray marks. The Latin text in the middle reads with errors of about one word in fifteen. The end is a list of Rolls volumes, readable.
Content note: Volume II of the Leicester canon's chronicle, whose later pages describe Wyclif, his disciples Nicholas Hereford and John Aston, William Swyndurby (Swinderby) of Leicester, and the Lollards' doctrines, from a hostile but close eye-witness. Volume I (to 1361) was not vendored. The Rolls Series notice at the head and a marked errata list are left in place.

THE CHRONICLES AND MEMORIALS 


GREAT BRITAIN AND IRELAND 
DURING THE MIDDLE AGES. 


PUBLISHED BY THE AUTHORITY OF HER MAJESTY’S TREASURY, UNDER 
THE DIRECTION OF THE MASTER OF. THE ROLLS, 


On the 26th of January 1857, the Master of the Rolls 
submitted to the Treasury a proposal for the publication 
of materials for the History of this Country from the 
Invasion of the Romans to the reign of Henry VIII. 


The Master of the Rolls suggested that these materials 
should be selected for publication under competent 
editors without reference to periodical or chronological 
arrangement, without mutilation or abridgment, prefer- 
ence being given, in the first Instance, to such materials 
as were most scarce and valuable. ; 


He proposed that each chronicle or historical docu- 
ment to be edited should be treated in the same way as 
if the editor were engaged on an Kditio Princeps; and 
for this purpose the most correct text should be formed 
from an accurate collation of the best MSS. 


To render the work more generally useful, the Master 
of the Rolls suggested that the editor should give an 
account of the MSS. employed by him, of their age and 
their peculiarities; that he should add to the work a 
brief account of the life and times of the author, and 
any remarks necessary to explain the chronology ; but 
no other note or comment was to be allowed, except 
what might be necessary to establish the correctness of 


the text. 
a 2 


4 


The works to be published in octavo, separately, as. 
they were finished; the whole responsibility of the task 
resting upon the editors, who were to be chosen by the 
Master of the Rolls with the sanction of the Treasury. 

The Lords of Her Majesty’s Treasury, after a careful 
consideration of the subject, expressed their opinion ina 
Treasury Minute, dated February 9, 1857, that the plan 
recommended by the Master of the Rolls ‘ was well 
calculated for the accomplishment of this important 
national object, in an effectual and satisfactory manner, 
within a reasonable time, and provided proper attention be 
paid to economy, in making the detailed arrangements, 
without unnecessary expense.” 

They expressed their approbation of the proposal that 
each Chronicle and historical document should be edited 
in sucha manner as to represent with all possible correct- 
ness the text of each writer, derived from a collation of 
the best MSS., and that no notes should be added, except 
such as were illustrative of the various readings. They 
suggested, however, that the preface to each work should 
contain, in addition to the particulars proposed by the 
Master vf the Rolls, a biographical account of the author, 
so far as authentic materials existed for that purpose, 
and an estimate of his historical credibility and value. 


Rolls House, 
December 1857.

The mob breaks into the Marshalsea, enters London, and 
proceeds to the Tower. They design to kill the Archbishop. 
The King invites the people to meet him, and grants them a 
charter, afterwards annulled by Parliament. The Arch- 
bishop and six others seized and beheaded. Attack on thie 
Savoy Palace; it is burnt with its contents; no plundering 
allowed ; death of some drunken rioters. Attack on the new 
church of Clerkenwell; destruction of Highbury manor. 
Attack on the representatives of law; murder of Richard 
Lyons. Quarrels among rioters. Next day they gather in 
Smithfield under Wat Tyler; their demands. Wat Tyler 
slain by John de Walworth. The King knights Walworth and 
others. An armed band surrounds the rioters; the King bids 
them disperse. Jack Milner’s address, Jack Carter’s, Jack 
Trueman’s. John Ball’s letter. Similar risings in Norfolk — 
and at Peterborough. Rioters dispersed and punished; church 
avenged. Measures taken by the Bishop of Norwich. Violent 
demands at St. Alban’s; general alarm. Report that the 
rioters were coming to Leicester; alarm at the news; prepara- 
tions for defence. Alarm increases; treasures of the Duke or 
Lancaster brought to Leicester Abbey, but the abbat dare not 
receive them. Duke of Lancaster serving on Scotch border. 
The Duchess flees to Pontefract Castle; is refused admission, 
and goes on to Knaresborough. Report carried to the Duke, 
who refuses to be disturbed thereby ; finishes his work in the 
North; obtains leave to enter Scotland ; then makes known the 
doings in England. His followers desert him. Reports of 
further devastations. Harl of Northumberland invites the 
Duke, but eventually fears to receive him. He begins to fear 
lest the King should be set against him ; a report to that effect 
spread by his rivals. He retires to Edinburgh, and is well 
received there; and is visited by Harls of Douglas and Dunbar. 
His reflections. He determines to put away his mistress, and 
does so. The King writes to the Duke; and commands the 
Earl of Northumberland to keep him safe; the duke declines

The other MS. Cotton. Tib. c. VII. (called A in the 
notes) is of 240 folios written across the whole page, and 
contains Knighton’s Chronicle only. This was the text 
from which Twysden printed, but it has been sadly 
- damaged in the fire of the Cottonian Library, so that in 
many places the margins and parts of the text are 
entirely gone. 

Both MSS. are in handwriting of the XVth century, 
but the former looks very like a copy of the latter. 
The misspellings in both are very frequently the same, 
and not unfrequently when a word has been written on 
the margin in A it is incorporated in the text of MS. 
But the scribe of the latter has sometimes been unable 
to read his text, and has left at times spaces for words 
which he could not make out. The notes in the first 
thirty pages of Volume I. will supply illustrations of 
what is here said. 

In A at the bottom of folio 8a are some Latin lines, 
headed Lamentum compilatoris, running thus : 

Sum ceecus factus subito caligine tactus, 

Non opus inceptum jam corrigo forsan ineptum. 
Me metuo dubium pro veris sepe locutum, 

Plus audita loquor quam modo visa sequor. 
Lector velle meum penses componere verum, 

Si minus est actum de me perpendite factum 


Me Deus allisit, cum vult sanare valebit,

Among« the MSS. at Lambeth there is a copy, in 
a seventeenth century hand, of Book F. and a few 
lines of Book II. of Knighton’s Chronicle. It extends 
over 33 pages. The MS. is No. 138, and the copying 
commences on page 78 with the “Lamentum Com- 
pilatoris.” It is probable, therefore, that it was made 
from our A, but the orthography is modified. It ends 
at tam multis validis congredt (Book IL., p. 55). It has

A) Compilatio Henrici de Knyghton Canonici Abbathice 
Leycestrensis de eventibus Anglice. In this copy too 
the spelling of the writer's name, as indicated by the 
capitals in Book I. was Henricus Cnitthon. 

The only value of these extracts is that they supply 
us with the text of the “ Lament.” But it would seem 
from some corrections made by a later hand! on the 
margin of A, that there must have existed a better text 
than either of those here used, though such a text is not 
now to be found.

From this examination of the text of Book II. it will

Turning to Book II. (Vol. L., pp. 269-479) we find it

which in this book also are made to form Knighton’s 
name, I am inclined to think that the breaks in the 
book were here made by the scribe in imitation of 
what the author himself has done in Books I. and II. 
This supposition helps, in part, to make intelligible 
Knighton’s words (Vol. 1, pp. 8, 4.) about his own 
arrangement of the books. In eleven out of the sixteen 
places where the illuminated letters of the proper name 
are found in Book III. no mark of a chapter is given in 
either MS. The scribe appears therefore to have amused 
himself by searching for sentences at convenient, in- 
tervals where the proper letter occurred in the opening 
word, and to have left these letters of the acrostic to 
be illuminated by another hand, as was usually done. 
At the seventh break, where the V of Henricus ought 
to have been displayed the illuminator seems to have 
thought he was one letter farther on in the name, for 
instead of Videns, both MSS. give Sidens.

XXXIV INTRODUCTION. 


It is at once clear from a comparison of this list with 
the printed text that up to the end of Chapter XII. all 
that is not taken by Knighton from Higden is copied or 
adapted from Hemingburgh, the change of order made in 
Hemingburgh’s material being due to a desire to make 
the narrative of Scotch affairs more continuous, and to 
range the events of continental history all into one 
narrative. 

In Book III., as in the previous book, several proper 
names have been found in Hemingburgh with a different 
spelling. These have been inserted in brackets in the 
Index Nominum at the end of Volume II. The name 
which (p. 345) is not given in either MS. of Knighton is 
set down as Bayon in Hemingburgh. 

On p. 350 Knighton intimates that he is copying from 
some authority, though he does not name it, only saying 
queere eodem libro capitulo 3. 

At pp. 388, 389 he mentions the name of Gisborne, 
after the account of the fighting in Annandale, as the 
place at which the church was burnt, Hemingburgh 
speaks of it as ecclesia nostra, as was natural for him 
who was canon of Gisborne. 

The reading Oxoniw on pp. 4383, 434 should be 
Exonic. But both MSS. have the word clearly written, 
and Twysden printed Oxoniwe. But it is manifestly a 
mistake. The same error occurs in the text ‘of the 
Chron. Angle, p. 15, under the year 1343. 

On p. 398 it is difficult to see why Knighton makes 
the note which he places at the close of the extract there 
given from the Ordinance of Pope Boniface about the 
differences between the kings of England and France. 
He represents himself as having diligently sought for the 
remainder of the document, but been unable to find it. 
_ The Papal award is given entire in Hemingburgh, IT. 
161-170.

The English King answered that his hands were full 
through the French King’s policy in aiding the Scotch 
rebels ; and to David Bruce he sent an answer to the 
same purport (p. 476). 

Knighton naturally notices in 1335 the burning of 
Cockerham manor and chapel with its books and 
muniments as being a possession of Leicester Abbey. 
In this year the Scots proposed to submit to England, 
and David Bruce and his wife were to reside in England 
till the death of Edward Baliol. But through the 
interference of the King of France, they held back and 
did not present themselves at the Parliament at the 
appointed time (p. 477). 

In consequence, the English King passed again into 
Scotland in 1336, and strengthened the fortifications of 
Perth, and also the fortresses of Stirling, Roxburgh, and 
Bothwell. The King’s brother, John of Eltham, died at 
Perth at this time. Edward is said to have made this 
expedition because troops from France were expected in 
Scotland, but after much marching and _ plundering, 
meeting with no resistance, he came back, and at

In 1344, Henry, Earl of Derby goes to France, for 
Charles of Blois was invading Brittany. This is a 
matter of interest for Knighton, as is also the murder of 
a clerk at Leicester, who was, it may be noted, a married 
man. The year was a fruitful one, and the Parliament 
gave the King liberal aids to be used for the good! of 
the realm, and to send an army against the Scots. 
Knighton notices the new coinage. In accordance with 
the wish of the nation a force under Edward Baliol was 
sent to protect the Scotch marches. 

A tournament” at Leicester, on the marriage of Matilda, 
daughter of the Earl of Derby, is noted by Knighton, 
who turns aside here to give an account of the family 
of Gilbert, Earl of Gloucester. 

The Pope sends a message that Edward shall cease to 
wear the arms of France, shall not disturb any ecclesias- 
tics who have been appointed by provision from Rome, 
and makes a large demand for money. The bearers of 
the message are sent away with a short answer. 

The Duke of Brittany, who had been the French 
King’s prisoner, escapes some time after Easter and comes 
to England.

two expeditions, first of the Earl of Northampton, along

INTRODUCTION. lix 
gives a long list of distinguished’ persons who were 
taken prisoners, while King David? was taken at 
Merrington and kept in Bamborough Castle till next 
year, when he was transferred to the Tower of London 
(2nd Jan. 1347). 

In the events of 1347 there are many details given by 
Knighton, of which there is no notice in the other 
contemporary chronicles. Such are the accounts of 
Edward’s refusal to allow any prisoners taken at 
Nevile’s Cross to be ransomed, and of the plundering of 
Scotland by the English immediately after the victory, 
in which proceeding he makes special mention of priests 
and people at Beverley and York as eminently active. 
He alone tells of the Irish rising prompted by the French 
and Scots, and of the aids granted to the King of England 
both now and at later period of the year (p.52). Of the 
latter he speaks from personal knowledge of what had 
been taken from Leicester Abbey and similar foundations. 

In the report of the campaign of the Ear] of Lancaster 
in Aquitaine, down to the taking of Poitiers, Knighton 
has something in common with the Chron. Angl., and 
partly with Walsingham, only that Knighton’s story 
implies some treacherous dealing from within at Poitiers 
while Walsingham ® speaks of an ordinary capture by 
storm. | 

After this follow several incidents peculiar to Knighton. 
The doings at David Bruce’s coming to London *; the 
storm-tossed return of Henry, Earl of Lancaster; the 
death of Eustace de Folville ; the execution of the Earls of 
Menteith and Fife; the introduction of some supplies

lxiv’ INTRODUCTION. 


Lancaster gave him. A truce, however, was agreed on 
for a time. oH 

There was a great mortality in the English ports, and 
Knighton records the number of deaths in Leicester. In — 
consequence of the ditliculty of visiting the sick a general 
remission was proclaimed for those dying of the plague. 
The evil extended to the flocks ;' all things fell in price, 
there were none to look after the crops, so that wages 
rose, and the affliction was so terrible that ‘By the foul 
death of England’ became a common? Scottish cath. 
The disease had the effect of checking invasion from 
Scotland. But out of it came a lack of clergy, and un- — 
qualified candidates began to seek ordination. The 
difficulty about wages became so great that legislation 
on the subject was deemed necessary. For men refused 
to work for the usual rates, and their refusal was 
punished by fine and imprisonment. The effects of the 
plague were disastrous: for houses fell into decay, there — 
were no servants to be had for farm labour, provisions 
increased in price, a remission of rents became general, 
and the services legally due from tenants attached to 
the soil lapsed; and as a consequence came dearth. 

The general absolution which the Pope offered would 
have drawn pilgrims to Rome, but the King forbad their 
going, and in consequence received a message from the 
Holy See, the tenor*® of which and the King’s reply 
show that there was much friction between the King and 
the Pope at this season. | 

The Earl of Lancaster was at this time ravaging in 
France, and specially the country about Toulouse. The 
Spaniards had with their fleet.made a descent in Estho- © 
nia, and in returning attacked ships belonging to England.

The Duke of Lancaster bounteously grants land for a 
park for Leicester abbey, and bestows on that. foundation 
the livings of Humberton and Hungerton, himself settling 
matters with the Pope about the presentations. The 


staple of wool was established in London! to the great 


advantage of the royal revenue. 

‘Knighton opens the year 1353 with a ane of some 
resistance at Chester to the circuit of the judges, to 
check which the presence was needed of the Prince of 
Wales and others of the nobles.. A fine was.paid to the 
Prince: of Wales by the offenders, and ina subsequent 
court of Trailbaston the judges appear to have. inflicted 
penalties with great severity. A second note is made of 
David Bruce’s vain endeavour to. bring about terms 
between England and Scotland, and (p. 76): the names 
are recorded of some who were to accompany him in his 
mission. The gift of 500 marks by the Prince of Wales 


to the Abbey of Dieulacres was thought to be as a tithe 
of what had been exacted from Chester. An expedition 
to Gascony, and a commission sent to Calais for the 


discussion of terms of peace are mentioned, as well as 


the laudation which was given to England by the Count 
-d’ Eu, for the kindness he had received asa prisoner there 
which brought suspicion: upon him in his own country 
_and he was seized and put to.death. There is a notice 


of the severe winter and of a tournament between 20 
French and 20 Gascons, in which the latter had the better.

Charles of Blois are the only part of this year’s events

King Edward was at Calais in Michaelmas, and the 
King of France with the ,help of Navarre proposed to 
come against him there. At this period Knighton 
- mentions the prevalence of a terrible mental malady, and 
also relates the trial and burning of some Minorite! 
Friars in the Papal dominions for declaring John XXII. 
to have been a heretic. This was because of certain 
decrees of his against the Franciscan order. 

Edward marched? to meet King John, who retired to 
Paris and the English returned to Calais. Here they 
learnt that Berwick had been taken® by the Scots, so 
the King hastened back, first going up to Newcastle, then 
to Berwick. Upon his arrival the enemy surrender 
(Jan. 24th) Edward Baliol resigns* his claim to the 
crown of Scotland. Edward marches forward into the 
country, first to Roxburgh, then to Edinburgh, Sir 
William Douglas refuses to submit, and on this account 
the King laid waste a large district. But the Scots had, 
in withdrawing, carried all provisions® away, so the 
English were compelled to retire. The King, however, 
tarried at Melrose with a few troops, while eae English-

In the Parliament of 1385, the duke obtained per- 
mission to go to Spain ‘in order to prosecute his claim to 
the kingdom which was made in right of his wife. 

The year was notable for the large number of French 
vessels, more than 80 in all, which were captured? by 
the English. 

Ere the duke set out on his voyage he took leave of 
the King and received costly presents, and it was by 
royal command that men were bidden to call him King 
of Spain, and pay him royal honours. The fleet sailed 
from Plymouth, and Henry his son, along with many 
other nobles, joined the expedition, which was also 
to receive help from Portugal? But by a marriage 
between the daughter of the duke* and the son 
of the King of Spain, war was avoided, and the ex- 
pedition came home. Though the story is thus com- 
pressed by the Chronicler into a very few sentences, the 
return was not till the year 1389. He does, however, 
mention a great incident of the voyage out to Spain. 
This was the relief of the castle of Brest, which was then 
besieged by the Duke of Brittany. The works raised 
about it were thrown down, and it was said that their 
dead were cast into the sea by the French and Bretons, 
lest the English should know the greatness of the 
disaster they had inflicted.? Several other sucesses are 
noticed as occurring in the great duke’s voyage, and the

The three Lords therefore gathered their forces, and 
attacked those who had come to the support of the Duke 
of Ireland near Radcote-bridge, and the Duke himself 
only escaped by swimming his horse across the Thames, 
while a great number of his supporters were drowned in 
the marshes. . 

Then the troops of the Lords go first to Oxford,! 
and afterwards to London,? where the Lord Mayor, 
Nicholas Exton, offered them the keys of the City.’ It 
was then agreed that there should be a conference 
between the Lords and the King, and for this object they 
came to the Tower,‘ and the King was induced to consent 
to the arrest of his favourites, and a great number of 
persons were arrested and consigned to custody in 
various places, and others were removed from their 
positions about the King. 

At the close of this very eventful year, the Chronicler 
mentions some singular appearances of fire, which were 
specially noticed in Leicestershire and Northamptonshire. 
He describes something very like magnified Will o’the 
Wisps. He also mentions a quarrel between ° the Welsh 
and Southerners in Oxford on one side, and the 
Northerners on the other, in which there was some blood 
shed, and in consequence the chancellor of the University 
was deposed.

The King removed from office in this year the chief

Truces were made with all the nations of the continent 
at this time. The next event noticed is the visitation 
of the diocese of Lincoln in 1892 by William Courtenay, 
Archbishop of Canterbury, who proceeded against the 
Lollards, and put many of them to penance. 

Two years before this the Duke of Lancaster had 
returned from Spain, and made a great hunting party in 
the parks round Leicester, while his son Henry went 
with a band of men to do service in Prussia. But 
England was in sore distress. Food and money were 
both scarce, so that the aldermen and citizens of London 
contributed for the purchase of food for the needy. 

The Parliament of 1391 dealt with the law of 
Mortmain, for the evasion of which means were soon 
discovered. 

The Duke of Gueldres urged the English King to go 
on with the war against France, but it was agreed that 
the Duke of Lancaster, with others, should first go to 
Amiens (in 13892) to confer with the French about peace, 
which was done next year (p. 321), and in the following 
year ” a truce was agreed upon for four years and four 
months (1398).

domestic history. With reference to Book V., I incline 
to the opinion, expressed by Dr. Shirley in a note to 
page 524 of the Fascicult Zizaniorwm, that it is not by 

the same hand as the rest. Knighton, according to the 

Lament prefixed to his introduction in A, was growing 
blind towards the end of his work. Such a calamity 
would account for the abrupt way in which Book IV. is 
brought to an end (see p. 123), and for the gap which 
occurs between Books IV. and V. The accession of 
Richard IL, with which Book V. opens, would form a 
fair starting point for anew writer, who would not 
feel called upon to notice the events of the closing years 
of Edward. | 

This new writer (who appears, ike Knighton, to have 
known a great deal about Leicester Abbey and the 
country round about) may have belonged to the same 
fraternity. If this hypothesis be accepted, it helps us to 
an explanation of the difficult sentence in the Introduc- 
tion (vol. 1. pp. 3-4) where Knighton describes the divi- 
sion of his book. That work (as we are supposing) con- 
sisted of four books. ‘The addition, made as is here 
assumed, raised the number to five. The words of the 
introduction had at first been IV. or quatuor, where we 
now twice over read quinque or V. This was noticed 
by a copyist (for we have not in these MSS. the original 
writing) and, having five books, he made the alteration 
of IV. into V., but did not see that he was leaving a 
difficulty for time to come in the words tertiam and 
gquartam, which still stand, as though the work were in 
four parts and no more. 

Dr. Shirley has also noted a difference of style in the 
lancuage of the two books, and a very slight comparison 
is needed to see that the manner of arrangement is 
different. In book V. the writer deals with his matter 
almost en bloc. He says what he has to say on each 
subject in a connected narrative and then leaves it, and

passes to something else.) He also has not as much 
zal for notinz details of prices, taxation, the assembling 
of parliament, and such matters, which are constantly 
recorded in the previous book. There is in both books 
the same interest shown in all which concerns the for- 
tunes of the house of Lancaster, and in the prosperity of 
the religious foundations of Leicester. But this interest 
would exist in all the members of the monastic body 
whose fortunes were so closely bound up with the Lan- 
castrian family. - 

In the notices of continental history this Chronicle 
needs to be largely supplemented from other narratives. 
The campaigns of Edward III. in France and of the 
Black Prince in France and Spain are recorded only ina 
general outline, and it is seldom that we find, as we do 
in the story of the meeting of Edward with Louis the 
Emperor (vol. IT., p. 5), more of precise detail in Knighton 
than occurs elsewhere. On the contrary, when he writes 
of the conflicts so constantly occurring at this time 
between the English and the Scots, he has often some 
particulars to record which are peculiar to himself. This 
probably comes to pass because the head of the house of 
Lancaster though more than once changed during the 
period covered by the Chronicle, was almost always 
concerned in what was doing. 

And in this connexion the Vth book is specially 
remarkable for the laudatory estimate which the writer 
gives us of John of Gaunt, so much differing in this

In book IV. Lancaster comes into no great prominence 
and is simply mentioned by name or title, but the 
writer of the Vth book omits no opportunity of lauda-

says (p. 146) that, at the time of Wat Tyler’s insurrec-

pacificus, dux prus, are the epithets which the Chronicler 
himself applies to him on the same page. The latter of 
these terms occurs almost at every allusion to him.t He — 
is pacis amator et. reformator (p. 146) and is several 
times spoken of as being under special care of divine 
providence.” He is pietatis robore fundatus (p. 148) 
and in his dealing with an enemy also he is pius, ut 
semper pius erat (p. 209). | z 

The duke’s departure for Spain, whither he went to 
claim the kingdom, affords a special occasion for glorify- 
ing him. He sets out on his expedition im nomine 
Domi (p. 207), and after the arrangements were made 
on account of which the claim was waived, the Chronicler 
tells with much pride (and his knowledge is gained from 
one of the duke’s own retinue), how the King of Spain 
met him with seven and forty mules bearing chests full 
of gold, as part payment for foregoing his claim. 

The only thing which the writer finds to regret in the 
duke’s doings is that he was always ready to stand by 
the Lollards (p. 193). But for this he has an apology. 
The pious duke believed them to be saints of God, by 
reason of their bland words and looks, whereby he, like 
many others, was deceived. 

For the Chronicler hates Wycliffe and his followers 
with a bitter hatred, and spends all the powers of his 
language in painting their evil character (pp. 181-187),

winding up with declaring them no better than followers 
of Mahomet. He knows little or nothing of the signs 
of the times. or the meaning of the Lollard movement. 
Nor has he eyes to see that Gaunt, who heartily desired 
to break the power of the clergy, found in Wycliffe and 
his preachers very useful weapons for his purpose. 

But it is for the light which he sheds upon the con- 
dition of England in his time, and on the changes 
therein which then began, that Knighton has a special 
value. And this remark applies very particularly to 
the matter contained in Book IV. We learn much from 
him about the fluctuations of prices! and the causes 
thereof ; of the great importance of the wool crop of the 
country, and the privileges attached to those places 
where the staples? were fixed for its purchase and sale. 
_ He records the prices of various kinds of grain, of wine, 
and of cattle, and gives a tragic account of the effects 
produced by the pestilential visitations of the time not 
only on the value but on the supply of food of all kinds. 
We gather much from him about the rate of wages, and 
the vain attempts that were made to regulate these by 
the artificial aid of legislation. On this subject he is 
rich in information, and we can see clearly how at this 
time the conditions of society were becoming entirely 
altered, largely in consequence of the devastations of the 
plague; how the labourer found that he could demand 
and obtain high pay for his services, and how for lack 
of population other results came about, cattle were 
untended, crops unreaped, and a pene recklessness 
prevailed. 

The workers who had been adscripts glebe secured a 
different position, and attained their freedom. Rents on 
every side fell, the owners of land making any sacrifice, 
if only they might keep it in cultivation. Relations 
which had grown up under the feudal system were

broken through, and the arrangement came in whereby 
the lands of the nobles and the monasteries were let to 
tenants at a yearly rental. 

Nor was it only in the classes of labourers, tenants, and 
owners of land that the effects of the pestilence made 
itself felt. There was in the Church first a dearth of 
clergy, and then a flood of ill-educated candidates came 
forward to fill the vacant places. This was about 1350, 
and 40 years later he paints for us a desperate picture 
of the condition of the country.’ A poor harvest in 1390 
was enough to reduce the people to the verge of starva- 
tion in spite of good years which had gone before. The 
money of the country had been drained away: the laws 
forbade merchants to carry their wool abroad for sale, 
and the prices they could obtain for it at home were 
miserably low. Food, he tells us, was not dear, but that 
was small consolation when there was no money where- 
with to purchase it. And this was the case to such a™ 
degree that the Corporation of London found it needful 
to contribute for the purchase of corn to be supplied at 
low rates to the people, so that the needy might be 
saved from perishing. 

Yet in the midst of these terrible narratives we have 
records” of increased extravagance among the wealthy, 
and of the need of sumptuary laws? to restrain the 
humbler sort from aping the manners and dress of their 
superiors in station. And we find a very graphic con- 
firmation in another Chronicle* of Knighton’s remarks 
about this rage for apparel. There the writer describes 
various newfangled garments which had come into 
vogue, and tells us of their materials and their cost, and 
adds thereto that such display had very evii effects on 
the character of their wearers, so that the writer declares 
he trembles lest there come again upon the land a 
terrible scourge of the Lord.

Knighton tells us much too about the taxation, granted 
by the Parliaments, or demanded by the King, for the 
various wars, destined to be all fruitless in the end, by 
which the national resources were being exhausted. 
Mostly the demands are for subsidies of war but at 
times for other needs, as when a princess to be married 
is to be supplied with a dowry. And the complaints! 
which found utterance in Richard’s reign prove that the 
sums drawn from the people at that time were often 
squandered upon royal favourites. The language in 
which taxation is spoken of is also instructive. Grants 
of Parliament are made, not always without demur, and 
then the phrase is concessa est. But now and again we 
have traces of other procedure in such expressions” as rex 
multarvit, rex fecit capere, rex misit clericos, and these, 
we may be certain, were agents who did not readily 
accept a refusal. 

A minor, but by no means trifling, drain on the 
resources of the nation was the cost of the visits of such 
Cardinals * as were sent from time to time from the Pope 
to treat for peace between France and England. Of the 
statute of Provisors (first passed in 1351) we have not 
much notice in Knighton, and the brief record of events 
at the end of Book V. omits any mention of its re-enact- 
ment in 1390, and also of the statute of Premunire of 
1398, though mention is made (p. 316) of attempts to 
evade the Mortmain Act, and of the legislation against 
them in 1391. ; 

The Chronicle closes in a time of comparative peace 
and good government, and of these years we are supplied 
by Knighton with very little history. But in the times 
whose events he has recorded more fully we see how 
the excessive war taxation, together with the loosening 
of the bonds of society by the Black Death in Edward’s 
reign, led up to the revolt under Richard when the poll

And the troubles of which Knighton speaks so much 
in the middle of Richard’s reign had their causes partly 
in the youth and weakness of the King, but were also 
largely the result of the rivalry and ambition of the 
nobles, some of them members of, and some very closely 
allied to, the royal line, and contributing weakness rather 
than ministering support to the occupant of the throne.

rentia exequlis celebratis die vili®. mensis Aprilis nuper

decrevimus introire, sed ex certis causis ad id nostrum

tione futuri pontificis tractaturi. Sequentique die luciferi nes-

ENGLAND. 


CALENDARS OF STATE PAPERS, &c. 


{ImprErtAL 8yo., cloth. Price 15s. each Volume or Part. | 


As far back as the year 1800, a Committee of the House of Commons 
recommended that Indexes and Calendars should be made to the Public 
Records, and thirty-six years afterwards another Committee of the House 
of Commons reiterated that recommendation in more forcible words ; but 
it was not until the incorporation of the State Paper Office with the Public 
Record Office that the Master of the Roils found himself in a position to 
take the necessary steps for carrying out the wishes of the House of 
Commons. 

On 7 December 1855, he stated to the lords of the Treasury that 
although ‘‘ the Records, State Papers, and Documents in his charge con- 
‘* stitute the most complete and perfect series of their kind in the civilized 
‘¢ world,” and although ‘‘ they are of the greatest value in a historical 
‘** and censtitutional point of view, yet they are comparatively useless +o 
‘* the public, from the want of proper Calendars and Indexes.”’ 

Their Lordships assented to the necessity of having Calendars prepared 
and printed, and empowered the Master of the Rolls to take such steps as 
might be necessary for this purpose. 

The following Works have been already published in this Series :— 


CALENDARIUM GENEALOGICUM; for the Reigns of Henry III. and Edward I. 
Edited by Cuartes Roserts, Secretary of the Public Record Office. 
2 Vols. 1865. 


Sy,LaBus, IN ENGLISH, oF RymMer’s Fapera. By Sir Tuomas Durrus Harpy, 
D.C.L., Deputy Keeper of the Records. Vol. 1.—1066-1377. (Out of 
print.) Vol. I1.—1877-1654. Vol. I1I., Appendix and Index. 1869- 


1885.

THE CHRONICLES AND MEMORIALS OF GREAT 
BRITAIN AND IRELAND DURING THE MIDDLE AGES. 


{Royat 8vo. Price 10s, each Volume or Part. | 


On 26 July 1822, the House of Commons presented an address to the 
Crown, stating that the editions of the works of our ancient historians 
were inconvenient and defective; that many of their writings still 
remained in manuscript, and, in some cases, in a single copy only. They 
added, ‘‘that an uniform and convenient edition of the whole, published 
** under His Majesty’s royal sanction, would be an undertaking honour- 
able to His Majesty’s reign, and conducive to the advancement of 
** historical and constitutional knowledge; that the House therefore 
** humbly besought His Majesty, that He would be graciously pleased to 
** give such directions as His Majesty, in His wisdom, might think fit, 
** for the publication of a complete edition of the ancient historians 
* of this realm.” ; 

The Master of the Rolls, being very desirous that effect should be given 
to the resolution of the House of Commons, submitted to Her Majesty’s 
Treasury in 1857 a plan for the publication of the ancient chronicles and 
memorials of the United Kingdom, and it was adopted accordingly, 

Of. the Chronicles and Memorials, the following volumes haye been 
published. They embrace the period from the earliest time of British 
history down to the end of the reign of Henry VII.

F. C. Hincreston, M.A. 1858. 


Capgrave’s Chronicle extends from the ereation of the world to the year 1417. As 


a re of the language spoken in Norfolk (being written in English), it is of considerable 
value.

Curonicon Monastertr pE Apinepon. Vols. I. and II. Edited by the 
Rev. JosrrH Stevenson, M.A., Vicar of Leighton Buzzard. 1858. 


This Chronicle traces the history of the monastery from its foundation by King Ina 
of Wessex, to the reign of Richard I. The author had access to the title deeds of the 
house, and incorporates into his history various charters of the Saxon kings, of great im- 
portance as illustrating not only the history of the locality but that of the kingdom. 


3. LIVES OF HpwaRD THE ConFessor. I.—La Hstoire de Seint Aedward le 
Rei. II.—Vita Beati HEdvardi Regis et Confessoris. III.—Vita 
Aiduuardi Regis qui apud Westmonasterium requiescit. Edited by 
Henry Ricuarps Luarp, M.A., Fellow and Assistant Tutor of Trinity 
College, Cambridge. 1858. _ 

The first is a poem in Norman French, ‘probably written in 1245. The second is an 
anonymous poem, written between 1440 and 1450, which is mainly valuable as a specimen of 


the Latin poctry of the time. The third, also by an anonymous author, was apparently 
written between 1066 and 1074, 


4, Monumenta Eranciscana. Vol. 1.—Thomas de Eccleston de Adventu 
Fratrum Minorum in Angliam. Ade de Marisco Epistole. Regis- 
trum Fratrum Minorum Londonie. Hdited by J. S. Brewer, M.A., 
Professor of English Literature, King’s College, London. Vol. I1.— 
De Adventu Minorum; re-edited, with additions. Chronicle of the 
Grey Friars. The ancient English version of the Rule of St. Francis. 
Abbreviatio Statutorum, 1451, &. Hdited by Ricnarp Howtetr, 
Barrister-at-Law. 1858, 1882. 

The first volume contains original materials for the history of the settlement of the 


order of St. Francis in England, the letters of Adam de Marisco, and other papers, The 
second volume contains materials found since the first volume was published,

Fascicunr ZizaANronum MacistRi JOHANNIS Wycuir cum Tritico. Ascribed 
to Tuomas Nerrer, of WaxnprEn, Provincial of the Carmelite Order 
in England, and Confessor to King Henry the Fifth. Edited by the

This work gives the only contemporaneous account of the rise of the Lollards. 


. Tur Burk or tHE Croniciis or Scornanp; or, A Metrical Version of the 


History of Hector Boece; by Winu1amM Stewart. Vols. I., II., and 
III. Hdited by W. B. Turnevty, Barrister-at-Law. 1858. 


This is a metrical translation of a Latin Prose Chronicle, written in the first half of the 
16th century. The narrative begins with the earliest legends and ends with the death of 
James I. of Scotland, and the “ evil ending of the traitors that slew him.’? The peculiarities 
of the Scottish dialect are well illustrated in this version. 

JOHANNIS CAPGRAVE Liner pe Intustrisus Henricis. Hdited by the 
Rev. F. C. Htnersron, M.A. 1858. 


The first part relates ‘only to the history of the Empire from the election of Henry I. 
the Fowler, to the end of the reign of the Hmperor Henry VI. The second part is devoted 
to English history, from the accession of Henry I. in 1100, to 1446, which was the twenty- 
fourth year of the reign of Henry VI. The third part contains the lives of illustrious men 
who have borne the name of Henry in various parts of the world. 


Historta Mownastrerir 8. AUGUSTINI CANTUARIENSIS, by THOMAS OF 
Etmuam, formerly Monk and Treasurer of that Foundation. Hdited 
by Cuartes Harpwicx, M.A., Fellow of St. Catharine’s Hall, and 
Christian Advocate in the University of Cambridge. 1858. , 


This history extends from the arrival of St. Augustine in Kent until 1191. 


Hu.Locium (HistoRiARUM sive TEmporis): Chronicon ab Orbe condito 
usque ad Annum Domini 1866; a monacho quodam Malmesbiriensi 
exaratum. Vols. I., II., and ITI. Hdited by F. S. Haypon, B.A. 
1858-1863. 


This is a Latin Chronicle extending from the Creation to the latter part of the reign of 
Edward III., and written by a monk of Malmesbury, about the year 1367. A continuation 
carries the history of England down to the year 1418. 


10. MremoriaAts oF Henry THE SEvENTH: Bernardi Andres Tholosatis Vita 


Regis Henrici Septimi; necnon alia quedam ad eundem Regem 
spectantia. Hdited by Jamus GairDNER. 1858. 


The contents of this volume are—(1) a life of Henry VIL. by his poet Laureate and 
historiographer, Bernard André, of Toulouse, with some compositions in verse, of which he 
is supposed to have been the author; (2) the journals of Roger Machado during certain 
embassies to Spain and. Brittany, the first of which had reference to the marriage of the 
King’s son, Arthur, with Catharine of Arragon; (3) two curious reports by envoys sent to 
Spain in 1505 touching the succession to the Crown of Castile, and a project of marriage 
between Henry VII. and the Queen of Naples; and (4) an account of Philip of Castile’s 
reception in England in 1506. Other documents of interest are given in an appendix. 


11. Mremoriats or Henry THE Firtnu. I.—Vita Henrici Quinti, Roberto 


Kedmanno auctore. I].—Versus Rhythmici in laudem Regis Henrici 
Quinti. IIJ.—Elmhami Liber Metricus de Henrico V. LHdited by 
Cuarues A. Cote. 1858. 


12. Munimenta GILpHALL& Lonponrens!s; Liber Albus, Liber Custu- 


maram, et Liber Horn, in archivis Gildhalle asservati. Vol. L., 
Liber Albus. Vol. II. (in Two Parts), Liber Custumarum. Vol. IIL., 
Translation of the Anglo-Norman Passages in Liber Albus, Glos- 
saries, Appendices, and Index. Hdited by Henry Tuomas Riey, 
M.A., Barrister-at-Law. 1859-1862. 


The Liber Albus, compiled by John Carpenter, Common Clerk of the City of London in 
the year 1419, gives an account of the laws, regulations, and institutions of that City in the 
j2th, 13th, 14th, and early part of the 15th centuries. The Liber Custumaruwm was com- 
piled in the early part of the 14th century during the reign of Edward II. It also gives an

26. DuscRipTIVE CATALOGUE OF MANUSCRIPTS RELATING TO THE HISTORY OF

Sir oe Durrus Harpy, D.C.L., Deputy Keeper of the Records. 
1862-1871. 


The object of this work is to publish notices of all known sourees of British history, 
both printed and unprinted, in one continued sequence. The materials, when historical (as 
distinguished from biographical), are arranged under the year in which the latest event is 
recorded in the chronicle or history, and not under the period in which its author, real or 
supposed, flourished. Biographies are enumerated under the year in which the person 
commemorated died, and not under the year in which the life was written. <A brief 
analysis of each work has been added when deserving it, in which original portions are 
distinguished from mere compilations. A biographical sketch of the author of each piece 
has been added, and a brief notice of such British authors as have written on historical 
subjects.

Domespay Book, or the GREATSURVEY OF ENGLAND OF WILLIAM THE CONQUEROR, 
1086 ; fac-simile of the Part relating to each county, separately (with a 
few exceptions of double counties). Photozincographed at the 
Ordnance Survey Office, Southampton, by Colonel Sir Hmunry Jamus, 
R.E., F.R.S., &c., Dimector-GENERAL of the ORDNANCE SuRVEY, under 
the Superintendence of W. Basrvi Sanprrs, an Assistant Record 
Keeper. 35 Parts, imperial quarto and demy quarto (186]-1863), 
boards. 


Domesday Survey is in two parts or volumes. The first in folio, con- 
tains the counties of Bedford, Berks, Bucks, Cambridge, Chester, and 
Lancaster, Cornwall, Derby, Devon, Dorset, Gloucester, Hants, Hereford, 
Herts, Huntingdon, Kent, Leicester and Rutland, Lincoln, Middlesex, 
Northampton, Nottingham, Oxford, Salop, Somerset, Stafford, Surrey, 
Sussex, Warwick, Wilts, Worcester, and York. The second volume, in 
quarto, contains the counties of Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk. 

Domesday Book was printed verbatim et literatim during the last century, 
in consequence of an address of the House of Lords to King George III. 
in 1767. It was not, however, commenced until 1773, and was completed 
early in 1783. In 1860, Her Majesty’s Government with the concurrence 
of the Master of the Rolls, determined to apply the art of photozincography 
to the production of a fac-simile of Domesday Book.

The first Part extends from William the Conqueror to Henry VIT., and 
contains autographs of the kings of England, as well as of many other 
illustrious personages famous in history, and some interesting charters, 
letters patent, and state papers. The second Part for the reigns of 
Henry VIII. and Edward VI., consists principally of holograph letters, . 
and autographs of kings, princes, statesmen, and other persons of great 
historical interest, who lived during those reigns. The third Part contains 
similar documents for the reigns of Mary and Elizabeth, including a 
signed bill of Lady Jane Grey. The fourth Part concludes the series, 
and comprises a number of documents taken from the originals belonging 
to the Constable of the Tower of London; also several records illustrative 
of the Gunpowder Plot, and a woodcut containing portraits of Mary Queen 
of Svots and James VI., circulated by their adherents in England, 1580-3.

J. Cameron, R.H.,C.B., F.R.S., and edited by W. Basevi SanpErRs, an 
Assistant Record Keeper. Part I. Price 21. 10s. 


The Anglo-Saxon MSS. represented in this volume from the earlier por- 
tions of the collection of archives belonging to the Dean and Chapter of 
Canterbury, and consist of a series of 25 charters, deeds, and wills, com- 
mencing with a record of proceedings at the first Synodal Council of 
Clovestho in 742, and terminating with the first part of a tripartite 
chirograph of the sixth year of the reign of Edward the Confessor. 


Fac-simines or Aneio-Saxon Manuscripts. Photozincographed, by Com- 
mand of Her Majesty, upon the recommendation of the Master of the 
Rolls, by the Drrector-GENERAL of the OnpNANCESuRvEY, Major-General 
A. Cooxn, R.E., C.B., and collected and edited by W. Basrvi SanDERs. 
an Assistant Record Keeper. Part II. Price 31. 10s. 

(Also, separately. Hdward the Confessor’s Charter. Price 2s.) 


° The originals of the Fac-similes contained in this volume belong to the 
Deans and Chapters of Westminster, Exeter, Wells, Winchester, and 
Worcester; the Marquis of Bath, the Earl of Ilchester, Winchester 
College, Her Majesty’s Public Record Office, Bodleian Library, Somerset- 
shire Archeological and National History Society’s Museum in Taunton 
Castle, and William Salt Library at Stafford. They consist of charters 
and other documents granted by, or during the reigns of, Baldred, 
Aithelred, Offa, and Burgred, Kings of Mercia; Uhtred of the Huiceas, 
Ceadwalla and Ini of Wessex; Aithelwulf, Eadward the Elder, Athelstan, 
Eadmund the First, Eadred, Eadwig, Eadgar, Hadward the Second, 
Zéthelred the Second, Cnut, Eadward the Confessor, and William the 
Conqueror, embracing altogether a period of nearly four hundred years. 


Fac-stmines of ANGLO-Saxon Manuscripts. Photozincographed, by Com- 
mand of Her Majesty, upon the recommendation of the Master of the 
Rolls, by the Drrecror-GENERAL of the Onpnance Survey, Colonel R. H. 
SrorHERD, R.E., C.B., and collected and edited by W. Basrvi Sanpers, 
an Assistant Keeper of Her Majesty’s Records. Part III. Price 62. 6s. 


This volume contains fac-similes of the Ashburnham collection of 
Anglo-Saxon Charters, &c., including King Alfred’s Will. The MSS. 
represented in it, range from A.D. 697 to A.D. 1161, being charters, wills, 
deeds, and reports of Synodal transactions during the reigns of Kings 
Wihtred of Kent, Offa, Eardwulf, Coenwulf, Cuthred, Beornwulf, 
Zethelwulf, A®lfred, Eadward the Elder, Eadmund, Eadred, Queen 
Kadgifu, and Kings Eadgar, Aithelred the Second, Cnut, Henry the First 
and Henry the Second. In addition to these are two belonging to the 
Marquis of Anglesey, one of them being the Foundation Charter of Burton 
Abbey by Atthelred the Second with the testament of its great bene- 


factor Wulfric. :

Fac-stmibes or Nationa, Manuscripts OF IRELAND, FROM THE EARLIEST 
EXTANT SPECIMENS TO A.D. 1719. Edited by Joun T. Gitzert, F.S8.A., 
M.R.LA. Pari I. is out of print. Parts II.and IIL. Price 42s. each. 
Part IV.1. Price 51. 5s. Part [V.2. Price 41. 10s. 


This work torms a comprehensive Paleographic Series for Ireland. It 
furnishes characteristic specimens of the documents which have come 
down from each of the classes which, in past ages, formed principal 
elements in the population of Ireland, or exercised an influence in her 
affairs. With these reproductions are combined fac-similes of writings 
connected with eminent personages or transactions of importance in the 
annals of the country to the early part of the eighteenth century. 

The specimens have been reproduced as nearly as possible in accord- 
ance with the originals, in dimensions, colouring, and general appearance. 
Characteristic exa1 mples of styles of writing and caligraphic ornamenta- 
tion are, so far as practicable, associated with subjects. of historic and 
linguistic jnterest. Descriptions of the various manuscripts are given 
by the Editor in the Introduction. The contents of the specimens are 
fully elucidated and printed in the original languages, opposite to 
the Fac-similes—line for line—without contractions—thus facilitating 
xeference and aiding effectively those interested in paleographic studies. 

In the work are also printed in full, for the first time, many original 
and important historical documents. 

Part I. commences with the earliest Irish MSS. extant. 

Part IJ.: From the Twelfth Century to A.D. 1299. 

Part III.: From A.D. 1800 to end of reign of Henry VIII. 

Part IV. 1.: From reign of Edward VI. to that of James I, 

In Part IV. 2.—the work is carried down to the early ee of the 
eighteenth century, with Index to the entire publication.
